oneSentence: A deepfake is a fabricated or heavily altered image, audio clip or video made to imitate a real person, scene or event convincingly.
plainExplanation:
A deepfake is a type of synthetic media: content made or changed by a computer model rather than recorded exactly as it happened. The input may be real photos, video clips or voice recordings of a person, plus text instructions or another video to copy. The output may show someone appearing to say or do something that they never said or did.

A common form is a face swap, where one person’s face is placed onto another person’s body in a video. Another form copies a person’s voice from sample recordings and then generates new speech. Some systems also create entirely new people or scenes that look realistic, even though no camera captured them.

Under the surface, a model learns patterns from many examples. In simple terms, it analyses how faces move, how lighting falls, or how a voice changes across words. Then it generates new pixels or sound waves that match those patterns. This can be done with different kinds of models, including diffusion models, generative adversarial networks and other media-generation systems.

People often confuse deepfakes with all fake media, but not every edited or misleading clip is a deepfake. A slowed video, a cropped photo or a false caption can mislead without using AI generation at all. What makes a deepfake distinctive is the use of generative methods to create or alter media so it appears authentic.

everydayAnalogy.title: A forged video portrait in a studio
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine a small media studio in Panama City preparing a historical exhibition. A technician has many real portrait photos of a famous singer, a separate video of an actor reading lines, and software that can combine them. The software studies the singer’s facial features and the actor’s head movements, then produces a new clip that makes it look as if the singer performed those lines on camera. Visitors who only see the final clip may think the recording is genuine.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: This analogy makes the process sound like a simple cut-and-paste studio trick. Real deepfake systems usually generate many tiny visual or audio details mathematically, frame by frame or sample by sample, rather than just layering one portrait onto another. It also does not capture voice cloning, fully invented people, or the fact that some deepfakes are detected by analysing artefacts and provenance information, not by noticing obvious editing.

visual.title: How a deepfake is made and why it can mislead
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this diagram, the reader should be able to describe the basic flow from source material to generated output and explain why realism does not prove authenticity.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. It starts with real source material, moves to a generative model, then to a synthetic output, and ends with viewer judgement and verification. Read from left to right to see how believable media can be produced from real examples and why checking the source matters.

steps.label: 1. Source material

visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains the process in four stages. First, real source material is gathered, such as photos, recordings or a script. Second, a generative model analyses patterns in that material, including appearance, movement or voice traits. Third, the model creates synthetic media that imitates a person or event. Fourth, a viewer encounters the result and may mistake it for real unless they verify the source, context or provenance. The main point is that realistic media can be generated from real examples, so appearance alone is not proof of authenticity.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow chart is shown instead of animation. Arrows connect source material, pattern learning, generated media and human response, with the same labels and example notes visible at once.

workedExample.scenario: A false video appears online two days before a city election, showing a mayoral candidate apparently admitting to ballot tampering.
workedExample.input: 20 public interview clips of the candidate, a clean audio sample from speeches, and a separate actor video reading a fabricated script.
process: The creator collects enough public footage to capture the candidate’s face from different angles and their speaking style.
A model is used to generate a face animation and matching voice that fit the fake script.
The generated face and audio are combined with the actor’s body and background to produce a 42-second video.
Viewers share the clip quickly because it appears urgent and looks like a phone recording.
workedExample.result: The video is convincing enough to confuse many viewers, but it is not evidence that the candidate actually said those words; investigators would need source checks, context and other verification.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN communications team monitoring social media sees a video that appears to show a senior official making a controversial statement about a developing crisis.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Staff need to recognise that realistic video can be fabricated and should verify source, provenance and context before repeating, rebutting or escalating it internally or publicly.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential footage, personal data, survivor testimony, security-sensitive material or internal recordings into an unapproved public AI service to test whether the clip is fake; use approved channels and human review.

whyItMatters: Deepfakes matter because people often treat photos, audio and video as strong evidence. If realistic media can be fabricated, then seeing or hearing something is no longer enough on its own. This affects journalism, elections, fraud prevention, public trust, reputations, human rights documentation and crisis response. For non-specialists, the key decision point is not learning to spot every fake by eye. It is learning to pause, check the source, ask whether there is independent confirmation, and use provenance or verification tools where available. Deepfakes can also be used in harmless or creative ways, but the same techniques can support impersonation, harassment or deception.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Every fake-looking video online is a deepfake.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Many misleading clips are simple edits, old footage reused in a new context, slowed audio, false subtitles or manipulated captions. 'Deepfake' usually refers to media created or altered with generative techniques that imitate reality, especially a person’s face or voice.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a deepfake looks perfect, ordinary people have no way to respond.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Visual inspection alone can fail, but people still have useful checks. They can look for the original source, compare with trusted reporting, check whether reputable accounts carry the same material, and use provenance or forensic review where available. The right response is verification, not guessing from appearance alone.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Deepfakes are only a celebrity problem.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Public figures are common targets because there is lots of source material, but ordinary people can also be harmed through voice scams, harassment, non-consensual sexual content or false evidence. The risk is wider than entertainment and affects personal safety, trust and reputation.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A deepfake is media made by AI tools to look or sound like a real person or event, even when the recording is invented or heavily changed.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A deepfake is a subset of synthetic media produced with generative methods that imitate identifiable visual or audio characteristics, often of a real person. Inputs may include reference images, video frames, speech samples, text prompts or a source performance. The system learns statistical patterns in facial appearance, motion, lip synchronisation, vocal timbre or scene structure, then generates new pixels or waveforms to create altered or fully synthetic content. Common implementations have included face reenactment, face swapping, voice cloning and text-to-video generation, using model families such as generative adversarial networks or diffusion models. The term is used widely in public discussion, but in practice its boundary with broader synthetic media is blurry, especially as modern generation tools can create realistic output without a traditional face-swap pipeline.

keyTakeaway: A realistic clip can be generated, so authenticity should be checked from source and context, not judged by appearance alone.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits the term 'deepfake'?
options: A video of a real speech uploaded with the wrong date in the caption
An AI-generated audio clip that imitates a minister’s voice saying words they never recorded
A blurry phone video that is hard to verify because the camera shook
A genuine photo edited only to improve brightness and contrast
quickCheck.explanation: The second option uses generative methods to imitate a real person’s voice and create speech that was never recorded. The other options may be misleading or altered, but they are not deepfakes just because they cause confusion.

contested: The exact boundary between 'deepfake' and the broader term 'synthetic media' is unsettled in public use. Some people use 'deepfake' mainly for face and voice impersonation of real people, while others use it more broadly for many kinds of realistic AI-generated media.
